title: China's AI models, led by Kimi, dominate open-source enterprise spending

China’s AI models, led by Kimi, dominate open-source enterprise spending
Chinese systems account for 89 per cent of spending on open-source models, but the category is small compared with spending on proprietary models
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Minxiao Changin Shenzhen
Chinese artificial intelligence models led by Moonshot AI’s Kimi family accounted for nearly nine-tenths of estimated global enterprise spending on open-source systems, according to a new study, even though proprietary US rivals continue to capture the vast majority of overall revenue.
The report, released this week by Silicon Valley venture capital firm Menlo Ventures, said Chinese AI systems accounted for 89 per cent of global enterprise spending on open-source models. Kimi led with a 61 per cent share, followed by DeepSeek at 15 per cent and Z.ai’s GLM series at 11 per cent.
By contrast, Meta Platforms’ Llama series, the leading Western offering in the category, accounted for just 7 per cent of open-source enterprise spending.

report.summary: Menlo Ventures report says Chinese open-source AI models, led by Moonshot's Kimi, captured 89% of global enterprise spending on open-source models.
report.background: The report lands as enterprises weigh proprietary APIs against open-weight models they can host or fine-tune. Open-source models appeal for cost control, customization, data residency and avoiding vendor lock-in, but they are only one slice of enterprise AI budgets; proprietary US models still dominate overall revenue. Chinese labs have released competitive open-weight systems and built developer ecosystems around them, while Meta's Llama has been the best-known Western open alternative. Menlo Ventures' estimate focuses on enterprise spending, not consumer usage or model downloads, so it signals where companies are paying for hosted or supported open-source deployments. The 89% figure should be read within that narrower category: it shows Chinese models' strength in open-source enterprise adoption, not overall AI market leadership.
key_points: Menlo Ventures estimates Chinese AI systems took 89% of global enterprise spending on open-source models. Moonshot AI's Kimi family led with 61%, followed by DeepSeek at 15% and Z.ai's GLM at 11%. That means three Chinese model families accounted for 87% of spending in this niche.

Meta's Llama, the best-known Western open-source model family, captured only 7% of open-source enterprise spending. The gap suggests that despite Llama's popularity among developers, enterprises paying for open-source deployments are increasingly choosing Chinese alternatives.

The open-source segment is small compared with proprietary models, and US proprietary vendors still take most overall enterprise AI revenue. So Chinese dominance is significant for open-weight adoption but does not mean Chinese labs lead the entire enterprise AI market.

Kimi's 61% share shows a concentrated market: one model family holds a clear majority, while DeepSeek and GLM trail far behind. Enterprise spending is a stronger adoption signal than downloads or benchmark scores because it reflects paid production use, though the report's estimates may not capture self-hosted or unbilled usage.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report suggests open-weight Chinese models have become the default choice in the paid open-source enterprise niche, pressuring Western open-source efforts and proprietary vendors on price and customization. Developers gain credible low-cost options they can self-host or fine-tune, but they must weigh licensing, security, data governance and support risks. Enterprises may adopt a mixed stack: proprietary frontier APIs for difficult tasks, Chinese open models for cost-sensitive workloads. Regular users may see cheaper AI features and more choice, but the effect is indirect because proprietary US models still dominate overall spending and frontier capabilities. The main takeaway is segment leadership, not a wholesale shift in the AI market.
report.tools: To follow up, watch Moonshot AI's Kimi model family, DeepSeek and Z.ai's GLM series, plus Meta's Llama as the Western baseline. Try models through Hugging Face, Ollama or vLLM for local deployment, and OpenRouter for side-by-side API access. For enterprise evaluation, compare hosted pricing, licenses, context limits and data-governance terms before adopting any open-weight model.
